summary:
Steve Ruiz, founder and CEO of tldraw, presents at the AI Engineer World's Fair about tldraw's AI experiments on an infinite canvas. Tldraw originated as a digital ink library and evolved into two offerings: tldraw.com, a free end-user whiteboard application, and tldraw.dev, an SDK for building canvas-based web applications. The canvas is React-based and can embed arbitrary web content including YouTube videos, CodeSandbox, Figma, Excel, and even tldraw itself recursively.

Ruiz demonstrates several AI projects. Make Real (end of 2023) uses vision models like GPT-4 with vision to convert wireframes into functional web applications with annotation-based iterative refinement. Draw Fast uses latent consistency models for near-real-time image generation from drawings. The main focus is tldraw computer, a visual programming environment where LLM-powered nodes accept inputs, run scripts (LLM prompts), and produce outputs connected by arrows. Built with Google using Gemini Flash, it supports cycles and loops—demonstrated by a pop song generator that runs indefinitely, creating songs, checking if they are about love, and sorting them. Ruiz envisions long-lived asynchronous processes running in the cloud for tasks like email sentiment analysis pipelines.

Ruiz also demonstrates a teach tool where AI acts as a virtual collaborator on the canvas, drawing shapes (not pixels) from text prompts and manipulating existing shapes—such as making a drawn cat blow out a candle, complete with generated smoke. This uses Claude as the backend. Ruiz emphasizes tldraw's advantage as a hackable canvas SDK with a runtime API that integrates well with other AI tools, and highlights community projects including a liquid simulation and Observable's use of tldraw. He closes by encouraging the audience to build something amazing, noting tldraw is only scratching the surface of this paradigm.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and tldraw background
sections.summary: Steve Ruiz introduces himself as founder of tldraw, which started as a digital ink library implemented in Excalidraw and evolved into an SDK for building canvas applications. He notes that if you build a canvas people can use, they will build cool things with it.

sections.title: Tldraw canvas capabilities and embeddings
sections.summary: Ruiz demonstrates tldraw.com as a free whiteboard and tldraw.dev as the SDK site. The canvas is React-based and can embed arbitrary web content like YouTube, CodeSandbox, Figma, and Excel. He embeds tldraw inside itself recursively and highlights canvas detail-handling like arrow routing and box corners.

sections.title: Make Real demo
sections.summary: Ruiz presents Make Real (end of 2023), which uses vision models like GPT-4 with vision to convert wireframes and diagrams into functional web apps. He demonstrates generating a stop motion app, annotating on top of generated output for iterative refinement, and fixing bugs by sending screenshots with source code.

sections.title: Draw Fast demo
sections.summary: Ruiz briefly demonstrates Draw Fast, which uses latent consistency models to generate images from drawings in near real-time. As the drawing changes, the generated image updates. Generated images can be flattened and interacted with on the canvas.

sections.title: Tldraw computer introduction and graph execution demo
sections.summary: Ruiz introduces tldraw computer, a visual programming environment where LLM-powered nodes accept inputs, run scripts, and produce outputs connected by arrows. He demonstrates a commercial-writing pipeline and shows LLMs performing nonlinear thinking—adding numbers and inferring numerical values from non-numeric inputs like the word octopus or a live camera feed. The project was built with Google using Gemini Flash.

sections.title: Tldraw computer cycles, loops, and async vision
sections.summary: Ruiz demonstrates tldraw computer supporting cycles and loops with a pop song generator that runs indefinitely—creating random songs, adding them to a list to avoid repeats, checking if each is about love (returning yes/no/maybe), and sorting accordingly. He envisions long-lived asynchronous cloud processes designed visually on the canvas, such as email engagement pipelines with sentiment analysis. The guiding philosophy is building a computer that works the way you thought computers worked before you knew how they worked.

sections.title: Teach tool and AI as virtual collaborator
sections.summary: Ruiz demonstrates a teach tool where AI acts as a virtual collaborator on the canvas, creating flowcharts from text prompts and incorporating existing shapes. The AI draws shapes (not pixels) from prompts like 'draw a cat' and can manipulate existing canvas elements—such as making a drawn cat blow out a candle, complete with generated smoke. This uses Claude as the backend. Ruiz notes tldraw's hackable canvas SDK with runtime API integrates well with other AI tools.

sections.title: Community projects and closing
sections.summary: Ruiz highlights community projects built on tldraw, including a Grant Cottrell liquid simulation using tldraw as a geometric control layer and Observable building with tldraw. He emphasizes tldraw is only scratching the surface of this paradigm and encourages the audience to build something amazing, offering to help with tools that make it easier.
